title: Nanak's teachings close
hook: a dialogue, an alphabet, a lament, the months, and three pillars

segments.voice: Yesterday, vand chhako: share, and eat, the sharing built into the meal. Your line was share first. Did you make the offer before anyone asked? Today we close the whole stretch of Guru Nanak's longer teachings. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

Suppose you could keep one sentence from the last several weeks, and only one. Which would it be? A circle of yogis on a mountain asking a stranger who he is. A pandit's alphabet turned into a poem. A child's writing tablet, one letter at a time. A lament for a city attacked and the women who suffered there. A year of months, each one aching. A ballad that holds every name up against a life. And three short phrases about remembering, working and sharing. That's a lot of road. Today we stand at the end of it and look back.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE TO KEEP.` → `A MOUNTAIN, AN ALPHABET, A LAMENT.` → `MONTHS, A BALLAD, THREE PHRASES.`

segments.voice: Lay the pieces side by side and one move keeps repeating. Guru Nanak takes something outward and turns it inward, without throwing it away. In the Sidh Gosht, the yogis wear earrings and a patched coat; he makes the Word the earring, worn within, and turns the coat into seeing the One in everything. In the Oankar, a learned man reads and argues; Nanak asks whether he has understood, and calls true learning reflection on the Name. In the Patti, a school slate becomes a lesson for the soul, one letter at a time. In the Babarvani, faith doesn't look away; he names the pain of ordinary people caught in an invasion. In his twelve months in Raga Tukhari, every season becomes a way of longing for the Beloved. In the Var in Majh, a name becomes a promise to live up to. And in the three phrases, a job, a meal and a breath each become practice. So that is Nanak's way, as these weeks have shown it. Not leaving the world. Living in it like a lotus in water, untouched, and making every ordinary thing point somewhere. One more detail before we cross into new ground. Read the Granth and you'll see Guru Nanak's hymns signed with his name, Nanak. The Gurus whose hymns follow his in the Granth signed them Nanak too, and a heading tells you whose voice it is: Mahala one, Mahala two, and on. The name carries on into the next voice. That's where we're going next, and it's today's line.
screen: `OUTWARD TURNED INWARD.` · `EARRINGS, SLATES, MONTHS AND NAMES.` · `LIVING IN THE WORLD, UNTOUCHED.` · `THE NAME CARRIES ON.` · then, large: `NANAK'S WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your favorite teaching. In the sit, let the breath slow, and let the stretch pass by again: the mountain conversation, the alphabet, the tablet, the lament, the months, the ballad, the three phrases. Don't choose the one that sounds wisest. Notice which one keeps coming back to you. Let it settle. Hold it on the breath for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru quietly on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nanak's teachings close. A dialogue, an alphabet, a lament, the months, a ballad and three pillars, all turning the outward world inward. Today's word.
Your line: nanak's way. Tell one person, tonight, the teaching you chose, in a single sentence. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet Guru Nanak's longer compositions, such as the Sidh Gosht, Oankar, Patti and Barah Maha, in kirtan and in katha at the gurdwara, sometimes studied over a run of sessions.

fork.setup: the yogis in the Sidh Gosht wear earrings and a patched coat as signs of their path. what does Nanak say?
options: take them off; they mean nothing.
the Word is the earring, worn within.
fork.reveal: he doesn't mock the signs; he turns them inward: the Guru's Word as the earring, worn where no one sees it.

original.note: the name that signs Guru Nanak's hymns, and the hymns of the Gurus after him.
